newsitem.title: USA: GM posts best North American profit in a decade.
newsitem.headline: GM posts best North American profit in a decade.

text.p: General Motors Corp., posting its best North American vehicle profits in a decade, said Monday it earned $1.8 billion from continuing operations in the first quarter, up from strike-crippled year-ago earnings of $800 million.
The March 1996 strike at two GM brake plants in Dayton, Ohio, slashed the year-earlier earnings by $900 million and forced the shutdown of 26 GM assembly plants and numerous components plants.
But GM roared back this year with first-quarter profits equal to $2.30 a share, up from 93 cents in the first quarter of 1996, as its sales grew to $42.26 billion from $39.24 billion.
The 1996 results excluded $219 million in profits from Electronic Data Systems Corp., which GM spun off last year.
The 1997 first-quarter performance exceeded Wall Street's consensus estimates of $2.09 a share. But GM shares slipped 12.5 cents to $52.875 in midday trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

Leading the way for GM was a $764 million profit from its North American vehicle operations, which compared with a year-earlier loss of $279 million in the first quarter of 1996. GM attributed $750 million of its year-ago strike losses to the North American Operations.
The improvements also came despite an increase in North American retail incentives to $860 per vehicle from $598 a year earlier.

GM's Delphi Automotive Systems parts unit, making its first quarterly report separate from the core automotive operation results, posted net income of $180 million for the period. The total included an after-tax charge of $50 million for the closing of a parts plant in Trenton, N.J.
Delphi earned a profit of $79 million in the first quarter of 1996, which included a $120 million negative strike impact.

GM Chairman Jack Smith said the first quarter performance, which was helped by the successful launch of new car models that cost less to build than earlier models, shows that GM's core North American business has "regained its basic earnings power."
"It's clear that we are moving in the right direction to further strengthen the corporation's financial performance," Smith said in a statement accompanying the results.
But GM's European operations continued to struggle under the weight of a fiercely competitive market, with operating profits falling to $94 million from $285 million a year ago.
The operating results excluded a gain of $55 million from the $1.1 billion settlement of GM's industrial espionage dispute with Germany's Volkswagen AG in January.

Including the gain, GM's International Operations -- which comprise the automaker's European, Latin American and Asia/Pacific operations -- reported net income of $317 million in the latest quarter, compared with earnings of $432 million in the prior-year period.

"The lower earnings in the first quarter of 1997 were primarily due to reduced volumes and higher sales incentives across Europe under intensely competitive market conditions, coupled with lower equity earnings, primarily from Saab as they await the release of their new 9-5 models," Smith said.
Saab Automobile AB is half-owned by GM and half by Sweden's Investor AB.
GM said its worldwide wholesale vehicle sales to dealers rose 11.6 percent in the first quarter to 2.19 million from 1.96 million in the year-ago period.

GM said its retail vehicle deliveries in the United States in the first quarter of 1997 totalled 1,123,000 units, resulting in a 30.2-percent share of the U.S. market. That compared with 1,152,000 units and a 31.2-percent share of the U.S. market in the first quarter of 1996.
In Europe, GM delivered 466,000 units to retail buyers for an 11.5 percent share of the market, down from 489,000 units, or a 12 percent share.
